questions.title: How exactly does 'Incremental Patching' distinguish itself from BPE tokenization in a generative setting?
questions.question_body: I am trying to understand the formal definition of incremental patching provided in Section 2.4. The paper states that BPE is not an incremental patching scheme because 'the same prefix can be tokenized differently depending on the continuation sequence.' I understand that BPE merges tokens based on frequency, but I am confused about *why* this violates the equation $f_p( oldsymbol{x}_{<i}) = f_p( oldsymbol{x})_{<i}$ during generation. If I am generating text token-by-token, doesn't the tokenizer look at the history? Why can't we just treat the BPE merge decisions as a sequential process that respects this property?

questions.title: What is the precise role of 'Hash N-Gram Embeddings' versus standard byte embeddings in the Local Encoder?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.2.1, the authors introduce hash n-gram embeddings where $e_i = x_i + 	ext{sum of hashes}$. My confusion lies in the interaction between these embeddings and the cross-attention mechanism. If we already have byte embeddings $x_i$ and then add n-gram hashes, isn't there redundancy? More importantly, how do these fixed-size hash indices allow the model to generalize to unseen byte combinations (out-of-vocabulary n-grams) compared to a standard subword tokenizer? Does the hash collision rate impact performance significantly given the small embedding tables used?

questions.title: Can someone clarify the FLOP accounting for Cross-Attention vs Self-Attention in BLT?
questions.question_body: Looking at Equation 10 for FLOPs estimation, I see terms for `Transf. FL` and `Cross Attn. FL`. The formula seems to imply that cross-attention flops depend on the ratio of queries ($r$) to keys/values ($k$). Specifically, for the encoder, it looks like $r = n_p/k$ (number of patches divided by something?). I am struggling to visualize how a single query vector per patch attending to multiple key/value vectors (one per byte) translates into that specific flop count compared to a standard self-attention layer where every element attends to every other element. Is the saving purely due to having fewer queries ($n_p$) than keys ($n_{bytes}$)?
questions., title: Why does increasing patch size lead to better scaling trends only when combined with larger model sizes?
questions.question_body: The paper claims in Section 5.3 that 'Patches Scale Better Than Tokens' because one can increase both model size and patch size while keeping inference flops constant. However, looking at Figure 4 (Fixed Inference Scaling), it seems that simply increasing patch size without adjusting model parameters actually hurts performance initially (the crossover point). Why does increasing patch size alone fail? Is it because reducing the number of global transformer steps reduces effective context length or information flow unless compensated by increasing hidden dimensions or depth? How does this relate to the claim that 'larger patch sizes appear to perform closer to BPE models at larger model scales'?

questions.title: Is there a risk of 'entropy drift' causing catastrophic failures in long documents with Entropy Patching?
questions.question_body: In Section 4.4 ('Entropy Model Context'), the authors mention resetting entropy context with new lines and using an approximate monotonicity constraint to suffer less from 'entropy drift'. What exactly constitutes entropy drift in this context? If a document contains long sections of repetitive code or structured data where entropy drops naturally over time, does the model incorrectly predict low entropy and create massive patches until it hits a boundary? How does this differ from Space Patching which relies on explicit delimiters rather than statistical thresholds?
